title: Type Aliases & Union Types
subtitle: type keyword, union (|), intersection (&), and discriminated unions
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Sometimes a value can legitimately be one of several types — a form field might be a string or null, an API might return a result or an error. interfaces can't represent 'either A or B'.
whyItExists.solution: type aliases give names to any type expression, including unions (A | B — either A or B), intersections (A & B — must be both), and mapped or computed types.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Unions for 'one of several types'. Intersections for combining object types. Type aliases for naming complex type expressions that you'll reuse.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use type aliases for simple named object shapes that might be extended by others — prefer interface for that. Don't abuse union types to represent a type that is always one specific thing.

explainModes.beginner: type is like a variable for types. type UserId = number — now UserId and number are the same thing. Union (|) means 'or': string | number means the value can be a string OR a number. Intersection (&) means 'and': TypeA & TypeB means the object has all properties of both.
explainModes.simple: type Alias = SomeType. Union: type ID = string | number. Intersection: type Admin = User & { role: 'admin' }. Discriminated union: each variant has a kind/type literal field — switch on that field to narrow. typeof Type[number] to extract union from const array. Template literal types: type EventName = `on${string}`.
explainModes.standard: Type alias vs interface: type can't be merged (no declaration merging), interface can. type aliases can express: unions (A|B), intersections (A&B), mapped types (Record<K,V>), conditional types (A extends B ? X : Y), template literal types. Discriminated unions are the TypeScript way to implement algebraic data types (Result<T, E>, Option<T>). The kind/type field acts as a discriminant.
explainModes.technical: Discriminated union exhaustiveness: TypeScript narrows via the discriminant in a switch — the default branch has type never if all variants are handled. Mapped types: type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }. Template literal types: type Getter<T extends string> = `get${Capitalize<T>}`. Recursive types: type JSON = string | number | boolean | null | JSON[] | { [key: string]: JSON }. Conditional types: type NonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T.
explainModes.deepDive: Distributive conditional types: type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never. Applied to a union, it distributes: ToArray<string | number> = string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. Infer keyword: type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : never — extract the return type of a function type. Template literal type inference: type EventMap = { click: MouseEvent, focus: FocusEvent }; type Listener<E extends keyof EventMap> = (e: EventMap[E]) => void.

questions.question: What is a discriminated union and why is it useful?
options: A union where all types are the same — for deduplication
A union where each variant has a literal 'kind' field that TypeScript uses to narrow the type in switch/if statements
A union that can only hold discriminated (unique) values
A union type that is deprecated in TypeScript 5
questions.explanation: A discriminated union is a union type where each variant includes a literal type field (like kind: 'circle' or kind: 'rectangle'). When you switch on that field, TypeScript knows exactly which variant you're in and allows access to that variant's unique properties. This pattern gives you type-safe variant handling similar to Rust's enums.

faq.q: When should I use type instead of interface?
faq.a: Use type for: unions (A | B), intersections (A & B), computed/mapped types, aliases to primitives (type UserId = number), and complex type expressions. Use interface for: object shapes that others will extend or implement, class contracts, and declaration merging (augmenting third-party types). In practice: start with interface for objects, switch to type when you need union/intersection/computed capabilities.

examples: type Action = { type: 'increment' } | { type: 'set'; value: number } — Redux discriminated union
type ApiResponse<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string } — Result type
type Theme = 'light' | 'dark' | 'system' — literal union for settings
